t: The Girl Who Asked for a Hairspray
b:
This is the story of a 13-year-old girl called Susie Maison who lived in America in 1955. She had a disease called asthma. She was worn out from using her asthma medicine over and over. What she used was a kind of device that produced a smoke-like vapour. In those days, apart from that, the only thing you could use was an asthma cigarette. (Those asthma cigarettes contained other forms of some of the medicines we use now. If you smoke the cigarettes we have today, it's heaven you'll be going to, not your asthma.)

It was when she was fed up that the light bulb went on in her head. She phoned her dad (who knows). Her dad, apparently, was the owner of a big pharmaceutical company. She cornered him and asked: "Why can't this medicine be made like a hairspray?" Out of all that love for his child (the love only dads have), that father worked with the chemists in his lab and designed the first modern inhaler. (If we'd asked for all this at home, we'd only have got a scolding: "This is exactly why we tell you not to get wet in the rain and not to bother the cat.")

How was the story? Well, it's only a story. Though it's told like this in many places, there's no historical evidence to confirm it. Still, this idea that sprang up in the mind of some blessed man or woman saves so many people today.

But this illness existed long before Susie's time. Ancient Chinese and Egyptian records talk about people who struggled to breathe. The one who named it "asthma" was Hippocrates. He believed it was connected to the environment, certain trades and metalwork. A man called Aretaeus wrote about something just like the illness we know now, and said you should drink owl's blood and wine for it (good grief!). Pliny the Elder said pollen was the cause and that a plant called ephedra was the cure. That's where the medicine ephedrine came from. It was used as an aerosol until 1910. Like this, scientist after scientist kept finding and telling us what causes asthma, right up to the middle of the 20th century.

It's there in Siddha medicine here too. They described it as an illness caused by an excess of phlegm, and called it Iya Eraippu Noi. Siddha medicine used the leaves of adathoda. Later, from that adathoda came a mucus-thinning medicine called bromhexine. (Our ancestors were no fools.)

By around the middle of the 1900s, many medicines that widen the airways (bronchodilators) had been discovered. But these are only a temporary fix. Only later did we learn that the lasting solution was steroids. Until then, many deaths continued. It was only around the 1980s that asthma was understood to be an inflammatory disease.

Let's see how asthma happens. Pollen, dust, cigarette smoke, viruses, exercise: any of these can trigger asthma. (Getting triggered over and over is its whole job!) Then the body's immunity sees it as an enemy. (Yes, as if there's no one else around, it shows off its strength for nothing.) As it fights the chemicals coming in from outside, the airway swells and narrows; as if that weren't enough, the muscle inside tightens too; and lots of mucus starts to come. Have you ever blown a poovarasu-leaf whistle? It only whistles if the tube is small. In the same way, when the airway is narrow, air going out makes a whistling sound (wheeze).

That's when we send in salbutamol by inhaler, which helps in the short term. The tightened muscle relaxes. But the one who keeps triggering is always around, isn't he, so that's when we send in a steroid every day. It goes in, says "let's just stay quietly in our corner", and takes the immunity into a meditative state where it doesn't lose its temper over every little thing. After that, even if it rains, our fellow won't care. (That doesn't mean you should keep poking at it. If the triggers are very heavy, you can get wheezing even while taking steroids. Then you need to be careful.)

In 2023 the WHO said 363 million people have asthma. It was the cause of 442,000 deaths. Many of those who died were in low- and middle-income countries. Asthma affects children the most. It is a chronic disease. It can be controlled, not cured. But nothing stands in the way of a child who lives with well-controlled asthma. Asthma won't get in the way of sport, studies or extracurricular activities.

To conclude –
Asthma is a chronic disease. But with control, you can live a full life. Avoid your triggers. Take your steroid inhaler regularly. When control slips, see your doctor; your medicine may need to be increased. Proper treatment gives a healthy life.

Archuthan Nithiyananthan
MBBS (Colombo)

Sources: WHO asthma fact sheet · Smithsonian: history of the asthma inhaler · A Brief History of Asthma · Medical News Today: asthma history · Global Asthma Report: Sri Lanka
note: Siddha is the traditional Tamil system of medicine. The poovarasu (portia tree) leaf is rolled into a whistle by children across Sri Lanka and Tamil Nadu.
